summary:
Fateheen-e-Khala (Conquerors of Space) is an interactive 3D open-world lunar landing and exploration simulator developed by students of Mazen School, Islamabad, for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Inspired by NASA’s Artemis missions, the game puts players in the boots of an astronaut navigating the Moon's south pole to find and validate safe landing sites for future lunar bases.

Exploring an infinite 3D terrain with day-night cycles and water-ice craters, players use an AR slope-detection visor, suit flashlight, and jetpack while managing suit battery drain from extreme solar heat and cryogenic crater chill. Using Sun and Earth compass arrows, players deploy a three-beacon triangulation system that projects a holographic landing zone and calculates ground slope to ensure flat terrain, sunlight access, and nearby ice resources.

Built with open-source NASA lunar data, the team developed and launched the web app using Google Gemini (game physics and prompt engineering), Google AI Studio & Three.js (3D WebGL environment), GitHub (version control), and Netlify (cloud deployment)—turning real lunar engineering challenges into an engaging, hands-on simulation.
details:
Fateheen-e-Khala (Conquerors of Space) is an interactive 3D open-world lunar exploration and landing-site validation simulator created by students of Mazen School, Islamabad, for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Built to simulate the real engineering challenges of NASA’s Artemis lunar missions, the web application puts players into the spacesuit of an astronaut surveying the Moon’s rugged south pole to identify, measure, and lock in safe landing zones for future human habitats.

What It Does & How It Works

Fateheen-e-Khala simulates an infinite, procedurally repeating lunar south-pole environment complete with shadowed water-ice craters, solar cycles, and realistic suit survival physics. Players complete a four-stage surveying and site-validation mission:

  1. Surface Navigation & Orientation: Because the Moon has no magnetic field for a standard compass, players use 3D Sun and Earth directional arrows alongside an automated day-night cycle to navigate across craters and ridges.
  2. Active Suit & Thermal Management: Players traverse low-gravity terrain using a Shift + Space jetpack boost and an F-key high-intensity flashlight inside permanently shadowed craters. Suit thermal physics dynamically drain battery power—penalizing the player when exposed to intense solar heat or cryogenic ice-crater chill—tracked live via a diegetic backpack battery ring and percentage readout.
  3. AR Slope-Detection Scanning: An onboard Augmented Reality (AR) slope-detection visor scans the ground ahead in real time to help players avoid hazardous inclines where a lunar lander could tip over.
  4. 3-Beacon Triangulation & Site Validation: Once a promising location is found, players deploy three physical beacons around the target area. The system projects a holographic landing zone triangle and computes the average terrain slope, verifying whether the site simultaneously meets safety requirements for flat ground, solar power access, and proximity to water-ice resources.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Hands-On Lunar Engineering Education: Transforms abstract aerospace parameters—such as landing-gear tilt limits, thermal extremes, and in-situ resource utilization (ISRU)—into intuitive, interactive gameplay that students and the public can immediately understand.
  • Accessible Browser-Based Simulation: Runs directly in any modern web browser without requiring heavy game-engine downloads or expensive simulation hardware.
  • Intended Impact: The project aims to inspire young learners in Pakistan and worldwide to engage with planetary science, while demonstrating how student teams can use open-source NASA datasets and modern web tools to model real-world deep-space mission planning.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Data & Research: Open-source NASA lunar terrain, south-pole illumination, and space-weather (DONKI) datasets from the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
  • AI & Prompt Engineering: Google Gemini to design realistic lunar physics rules, thermal drain equations, navigation mechanics, and structured development prompts.
  • 3D Engine & Frontend Stack: Google AI Studio to build the standalone web application using HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js (WebGL) for 3D terrain rendering, lighting, and holographic effects.
  • Version Control & Cloud Hosting: GitHub for source-code management and collaborative iteration, paired with Netlify for instant cloud deployment and live hackathon demonstrations.
  • Hardware Setup: Developed and tested on student laptops (such as HP ProBooks) and designed to run smoothly across standard laptops, tablets, and classroom computers.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered by the Team

  • Diegetic UI Over Cluttered HUDs: Rather than crowding the screen with arcade-style health bars, the team creatively built a diegetic backpack battery ring directly onto the astronaut's suit and used holographic ground projections so all critical telemetry feels native to the lunar environment.
  • Multi-Variable Landing Trade-Offs: The team factored in the real engineering conflict of the lunar south pole—landing sites need sunlight for solar power and flat terrain for safe touchdown, yet must sit close to freezing, pitch-black craters where water ice is trapped—forcing players to balance thermal battery drain against resource proximity.
  • Navigation Without GPS or Magnetism: Recognizing that traditional compasses fail on the Moon, the team incorporated Earth-in-the-sky and Sun-angle indicators, teaching players how real lunar astronauts orient themselves on the surface.
